name: Malaquías Peña
title: Associate Research Professor
affiliation: Civil and Environmental Engineering and Eversource Energy Center, University of Connecticut
bio: Malaquías Peña is an Associate Research Professor at the University of Connecticut, associated with the Eversource Energy Center and Civil and Environmental Engineering. His research asks how incomplete observations and models can support reliable predictions of interacting Earth and infrastructure systems.

He connects nonlinear dynamics and multiscale predictability with weather and climate prediction, data assimilation, digital twins, and infrastructure resilience. His published work spans coupled prediction, forecast uncertainty, offshore wind, electricity loads, and weather-informed power-system analysis. Current work examines compact dynamical representations, scientific machine learning, hierarchical inference, and the value of environmental information for engineering decisions.

Before joining UConn in 2017, he spent more than a decade at NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Prediction, contributing to the development of GEFS, CFSv2 and the UFS. He holds a Ph.D. in Meteorology from the University of Maryland and founded UConn's graduate Power Grid Modernization Certificate.
interests: Coupled data assimilation and digital twins
Scientific machine learning and hybrid AI–NWP

Two papers accepted for oral presentation at ACDSA 2027: a reduced-order digital twin for moving marine infrastructure (with A. Fontanez) and wind power ramp detection in ensemble forecasts (with A. Prevezianos, A. Unlu and E. Anagnostou).
New preprint: Logit–Koopman coordinates for scale-resolved forecast-error growth in a three-level Lorenz-96 system, arXiv:2610.34779, submitted to Chaos.
Seminar at the NOAA NCEP Environmental Modeling Center on coupled coastal wind–wave–current analysis with P. Mitsopoulos.
Impact of Assimilating Remote Sensing Observations on Wind and Wave Analysis Offshore of the Contiguous United States published in Remote Sensing.
Preprint revised: When is logistic error growth a spectral reduction?, arXiv:2608.26492, submitted to Nonlinear Processes in Geophysics.
Talk on multi-theory generative ensembles of the MJO at the 50th NOAA Climate Diagnostics and Prediction Workshop.
Talk on quantum-scan data assimilation at the US CLIVAR workshop on quantum computing and sensing for weather and climate.
Talk on hierarchy-native EO foundation models for digital twins at the 2nd ESA–NASA Workshop on AI Foundation Models for Earth Observation.
areas: Mathematical foundations of multiscale predictability, forecast-error growth, Logit–Koopman representations, and coarse graining. Which dynamical information does a reduced model preserve, and when can learning distinguish mechanisms that produce similar aggregate behavior?
Weather and climate prediction across interacting time and space scales: coupled ocean–atmosphere dynamics, turbulence closures, subseasonal variability, offshore wind and wind–wave–current analysis.
Hierarchical Data Assimilation and Digital Twins

Combining heterogeneous observations and model information across scales: decentralized estimation, learned priors, uncertainty calibration, and digital twins tested for information sharing, physical consistency and prediction under missing observations.
Environmental sensing and local computation for energy, water, coastal and marine infrastructure exposed to hazards, including quantum-enhanced and on-sensor approaches.
